title: Crises affect social cohesion through changing dependence, power asymmetries, interests, and the perceived legitimacy of cooperation
source_unit: Koster, Lang, and Van Lange, Interdependence explains how and when crises impact social cohesion, Communications Psychology 2026
geography: Theory-guided review drawing on evidence across natural hazards, pandemics, economic crises, and wars in multiple national and community contexts

observations.period: 2026 conceptual review; definition of social cohesion

denominator.unit: theory-guided review of social cohesion across crisis contexts

horizontal_cohesion.value: trust, solidarity, shared identity, cooperation, participation, and norm compliance among individuals and groups

vertical_cohesion.value: trust in and perceived legitimacy of governing institutions, including whether people view government responses as effective and fair

societal_level.value: cohesion is treated as an emergent societal pattern arising from person-person, group-group, and person-institution interactions rather than a single individual attitude

crisis_difference.value: the review argues that crises cannot be assumed to have one general effect on cohesion because their scope, duration, salience, distribution, and collective-action demands differ

observations.method: Theory-guided interdisciplinary review grounded in interdependence theory, social exchange theory, game theory, behavioral-science evidence, and studies of four crisis types.
observations.uncertainty: The framework organizes heterogeneous evidence and generates testable predictions; it is not a pooled causal estimate or a validated universal crisis-prediction model.
observations.subgroup: Individuals, groups, communities, governments, vulnerable populations, and institutions involved in crisis response and cooperation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Social cohesion may be defined and measured differently across disciplines and societies; stronger cohesion within a group can coexist with exclusion or conflict across groups.

observations.period: 2026 conceptual review; interdependence dimensions during crises

denominator.unit: core interdependence dimensions identified by the review

mutual_dependence.value: the degree to which people influence one another's outcomes can increase cooperation when mutual help is tangible and perceived as necessary

asymmetry.value: unequal dependence and vulnerability can make some groups bear greater costs while others retain more capacity and power

interests.value: corresponding interests support cooperation, while conflicting interests over safety, resources, freedom, or distribution can undermine cohesion

government_route.value: crises often increase citizens' dependence on government and government dependence on compliance, creating either legitimacy or resentment depending on perceived competence and fairness

observations.method: Conceptual synthesis applying interdependence theory to horizontal and vertical social relations during crisis response.
observations.uncertainty: The dimensions are analytically separable but interact in practice; the review does not provide a single operational index or estimate of their relative causal importance.
observations.subgroup: Groups differently exposed to crisis harms, resource scarcity, government mandates, economic loss, or response burdens.
observations.counterinterpretation: Perceived dependence may matter more than objective dependence, and shared identity or ideology can alter whether unequal burdens are interpreted as solidarity or exploitation.

denominator.unit: crisis types reviewed: natural hazards, pandemics, economic crises, and wars

natural_hazards.value: short, immediate disasters can increase local cooperation and solidarity, while prolonged or uneven hazards can intensify competition and conflict

pandemics.value: early shared vulnerability can mobilize prosocial behavior, while prolonged restrictions, misinformation, polarization, and unequal costs can weaken cohesion

economic_crises.value: financial strain and unemployment can increase dependence on social networks and government while widening asymmetries and scapegoating risks

wars.value: war can generate immediate within-group solidarity through necessity while undermining broader trust, institutions, and relationships through violence, displacement, and conflicting identities

observations.method: Review of empirical and theoretical literature across four crisis types, including surveys, behavioral evidence, field studies, meta-analyses, and historical cases.
observations.uncertainty: The review emphasizes context and timing; these pathways are conditional propositions rather than universal predictions for every disaster, pandemic, economic downturn, or war.
observations.subgroup: Crisis-affected communities, vulnerable households, marginalized groups, displaced people, public institutions, and groups with different exposure and response capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same crisis can produce solidarity and exclusion simultaneously, and observed cohesion may reflect coercion, survival necessity, or suppression rather than durable trust.

denominator.unit: review-derived framework for crisis research and response

coordination_mode.value: bottom-up voluntary cooperation is proposed as more likely to strengthen cohesion than top-down enforcement when burdens and legitimacy are contested

inequality_route.value: reducing asymmetry in dependence and conflicts of interest is identified as central to preserving cohesion

social_infrastructure.value: neighbor contact, community facilities, shared activities, emergency resources, and local organizations can create repeated settings for cooperation and resilience

research_design.value: the authors recommend combining experiments, surveys, interviews, behavioral games, historical, archival, and ethnographic approaches to test crisis-specific predictions

observations.method: Authors' synthesis of implications and proposed convergent research strategy.
observations.uncertainty: The policy propositions are theory-informed and require crisis-specific evaluation; voluntary coordination is not always feasible and top-down action may sometimes protect vulnerable groups or reduce harm.
observations.subgroup: Local governments, emergency managers, community organizations, public-health systems, households, and groups with unequal crisis exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Community-led response can reproduce local exclusion or shift unpaid burdens onto vulnerable people; infrastructure without fair distribution may deepen rather than reduce asymmetry.

related_sources.claim: Peer-reviewed Communications Psychology article proposing an interdependence framework for how natural hazards, pandemics, economic crises, and wars affect social cohesion.
Open-access full-text repository version with the review's theory, crisis pathways, broader implications, and references.

boundary: This record adds a crisis-mechanism route from changing mutual dependence, unequal vulnerability, conflicting interests, and coordination mode through horizontal and vertical social cohesion. It is a theory-guided review and hypothesis framework, not a pooled causal estimate, crisis forecast, or claim that any crisis has one uniform social effect.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Publisher and open-access full-text sources reviewed for the cohesion definition, four crisis typology, interdependence dimensions, differentiated pathways, policy implications, and proposed empirical tests.
